questions.q: For positive a and b, gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) equals:
questions.e: gcd(4, 6) × lcm(4, 6) = 2 × 12 = 24 = 4 × 6. Each prime's smaller and larger exponents add up to its total in a × b.

questions.q: Why does Euclid's step gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) work?
o: It only works when a is even
Because b is always smaller than a
Any common divisor of a and b also divides a % b = a − k·b
questions.h: Write a % b as a − k × b.
questions.e: If d divides a and b, it divides a − k·b = a % b, and the reverse also holds. So both pairs have the same common divisors and the same GCD.

questions.q: This function should return the GCD of a and b using a loop. Which line goes in the blank?
questions.e: The pair moves one step: b becomes the new a, and the remainder r becomes the new b. The last option computes a % b after a has already changed.

questions.q: This recursive function should return the GCD of a and b. Which call goes in the blank?
questions.h: Same step as the loop: (a, b) → (b, a % b).
questions.e: gcdRec(b, a % b) shrinks the pair each call until b = 0. gcdRec(a % b, b) keeps the same b forever and never reaches the base case.

questions.h: Make the number smaller before you multiply.
questions.e: Dividing first keeps the intermediate value at most the LCM itself. a * b can overflow even when the LCM fits.

questions.q: This function should return the GCD of a and b. For a = 48, b = 18 it returns 18 instead of 6. What is wrong?
o: It should return b instead of a
It needs a < b at the start
a is overwritten before a % b is computed; save r = a % b first
questions.h: After a = b, what is a % b?
questions.e: Once a = b, a % b is always 0, so the loop ends after one step with a = 18. Compute r = a % b first, then shift: a = b; b = r;

questions.q: This function should return the LCM of a and b. For a = b = 100000 (LCM 100000) it returns a wrong number. What is the fix?
o: Divide first, a / gcd(a, b) * b, and use long long
questions.e: a * b = 10^10 overflows int before the division happens. Divide first and use long long.

questions.q: This function should return the GCD of all the numbers in v. For {12, 18, 24} it returns 1 instead of 6. What is the fix?
o: Write gcd(x, g) instead of gcd(g, x)
Start g at 0 (gcd(0, x) = x) or at v[0]
questions.e: gcd(1, x) = 1, so starting at 1 locks the answer at 1. gcd(0, x) = x, which makes 0 the right starting value.

questions.q: This function returns the GCD of a and b. What does it return for a = 0, b = 7?
questions.h: First call: b = 7, so the next call is gcdRec(7, 0 % 7).
questions.e: gcdRec(0, 7) → gcdRec(7, 0) → 7. Every number divides 0, so gcd(0, x) = x.

questions.q: This function should return the GCD of a and b, which is always positive. For a = 12, b = −18 it returns −6. What is the safest fix?
o: Take absolute values first: a = llabs(a), b = llabs(b)
questions.h: In C++ the sign of a % b follows a.
questions.e: Negative inputs can leave a negative result. The GCD is defined as positive, so work on llabs(a) and llabs(b).

questions.q: a and b are up to 10^9. Does lcm(a, b) fit in a long long?
o: Yes, it even fits in an int
Only if a and b are prime
questions.h: The LCM is at most a × b.
questions.e: lcm ≤ a × b ≤ 10^18, and long long holds up to about 9.2 × 10^18. Compute it as a / gcd(a, b) * b.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of Euclid's algorithm?
questions.h: In every two steps the smaller number at least halves.
questions.e: The numbers shrink at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers grow, so even for 10^18 it takes fewer than 100 steps.

questions.q: What extra space do gcdRec and gcdIter use?
o: gcdRec: O(log min(a, b)) stack; gcdIter: O(1)
questions.h: Each recursive call stays on the stack until the base case.
questions.e: The recursion is as deep as the number of Euclid steps, O(log min(a, b)). The loop only keeps a, b and r.
